title: Benchmarks
one_line_goal: Fair, repeatable tests vs Chrome, Edge and plain Tauri; first data collected
summary: Build a test bench that compares Ferrum with Chrome, Edge and a bare Tauri app under identical conditions. Check it against itself to learn the noise level, write predictions down in advance, then run the first test campaign. Data is only collected here; it is interpreted in P8.

tasks.title: Bare Tauri app to compare against
tasks.chain: We must show what Ferrum adds over plain Tauri → build a minimal app on the same Tauri and WebView2 versions with no Ferrum features → differences can be credited to Ferrum's design.
tasks.check: It builds and loads a test page; a version comparison with Ferrum shows only intended differences.

tasks.title: Ten local test workloads
tasks.chain: Results must not depend on live websites → build ten local workloads (simple page, heavy web app, huge page, scrolling, many navigations, video, graphics, several active tabs, many background tabs, close and restore) → every product sees exactly the same content.
tasks.check: Each workload has its page and an equivalence check; content is identical across two server starts.

tasks.title: A few real websites as extras
tasks.chain: Local pages may not reflect real use → pick a short list of public sites without login, with the visit date recorded → a reality check, clearly labelled extra, never the main result.
tasks.check: A dry run records the response and page size for each site; no results drawn from it.

tasks.title: Fair settings for each product
tasks.chain: Chrome and Edge have built-in resource savers → record every relevant setting per product in versioned files, never switching their savers off just to help Ferrum → the comparison is fair and anyone can check it.
tasks.check: Every settings file passes a format check; a diff report shows only the documented differences.

tasks.title: Test runner
tasks.chain: Trial order and leftovers can bias results → a Rust runner shuffles trials with a recorded seed, starts each product fresh with a clean profile, tracks all its processes, and records every trial including failures → runs are fair, resumable and complete.
tasks.check: The same seed gives the same plan; a test confirms child processes are tracked and failures recorded.

tasks.title: Scripts that drive each workload
tasks.chain: Each product must be driven the same way → one browser-automation script (Playwright) per workload, connecting to every product through the same debugging channel → differences come from the products, not the driver.
tasks.check: Each script runs once on each product, or the unsupported feature is named and recorded.

tasks.title: Record the setup and pin versions
tasks.chain: A silent browser update mid-campaign would spoil the data → record Windows build, product versions, power plan and background apps for each run, and pin browser versions → any change is caught and flagged.
tasks.check: A dry-run record has every field; a test flags a version change between two trials.

tasks.title: Smoothness measurement
tasks.chain: Smooth scrolling and animation matter to users → measure frame timing with a Windows tool (PresentMon) and long-frame data inside the page → smoothness can be compared, or marked unsupported for a product.
tasks.check: A scrolling dry run gives frame data for each product, or the product is marked unsupported.

tasks.title: Energy, only if it can be measured honestly
tasks.chain: Energy use is worth reporting but hard to measure → if you approve, a separate admin-level reader collects CPU energy counters (labelled modelled, CPU only), or a wall-power meter is used → otherwise energy is marked unsupported, never estimated.
tasks.check: A dry run gives energy samples with units, or the energy measurements show unsupported with the reason.

tasks.title: Statistics pipeline
tasks.chain: Numbers need honest statistics → a Python pipeline computes averages, spread, confidence ranges, effect sizes and corrections for many comparisons, plus plots → the analysis is repeatable to the byte.
tasks.check: Tests on made-up data with known answers pass; two runs give identical output.

tasks.title: Measure the noise level
tasks.chain: Some variation is just noise → run one product against itself (an A/A test) plus short pilots → we know the smallest real difference we can detect and set the trial count for each experiment.
tasks.check: A/A data saved; noise level reported; each experiment page states its trial count and why.

tasks.title: Write predictions before testing
tasks.chain: Deciding what counts as success after seeing data is biased → write each prediction and its meaningful-difference threshold first, and you approve them → results cannot be bent to fit.
tasks.check: Every prediction is recorded and approved by you before the first campaign starts.

tasks.title: First test campaign
tasks.chain: The bench is ready and checked → run the footprint, startup, page-load, smoothness, reliability, security-cost and isolation-cost experiments (and energy if supported) on Chrome, Edge, bare Tauri and Ferrum without sleeping → raw data for P8 and a reference for P7.
tasks.check: Each experiment has a complete raw-data folder with every trial and checksums; no results stated yet.

tasks.title: Reproduction guides
tasks.chain: Others must be able to repeat our tests → write how-to guides for benchmarking and for reproducing a campaign on a clean PC → the research can be checked independently.
tasks.check: Following the guide on a fresh copy for one workload gives a valid run record.

tasks.title: Reading: benchmarking and statistics
tasks.chain: Methods must follow good practice → read the literature on benchmark methods and performance statistics → the method pages cite it.
tasks.check: New research notes saved; method pages cite them.

tasks.title: Gate and your review
tasks.chain: All tasks done → the gate script runs every check and saves the evidence → you review the first campaign and approve; only then does P7 start.
tasks.check: All evidence files exist, the wiki check is clean, and you approve the end of P6.

test_gate.explanation: Code and tests pass → settings are proven fair → test pages and analysis give the same output every time → noise level known → you approve the predictions and check the PC → first campaign data is complete → you approve. Only then does P7 start.

rows.proves: Code is tidy and warning-free, all automatic tests pass, and the release build works.
Third-party libraries have acceptable licences and no known security problems.
Products differ only in the documented ways.
Test pages and the analysis give identical results on every run.
Noise level measured; trial counts justified.
Every planned trial recorded, failures included, none dropped.
Security, tabs and browsing tests still pass.
The plan pages are consistent and have no broken links.
You confirm no Chrome or Edge saver was switched off to help Ferrum.
You approved the predictions before any comparison ran.
Power plan, display and background apps are set as the guide says.
